concepts.label: Federalism vs Unitary System
concepts.cardText: Federalism is a system of government in which power is divided between a central authority and its various constituent units. Under a unitary system, the central government can pass on orders to the provincial or local government. In a federal system, it cannot: the state government has powers of its own for which it is not answerable to the central government.
concepts.hint: In which system can the central government pass on orders to the provinces?
concepts.probe: What is the main difference between a federal and a unitary form of government? Give an example.
concepts.causeChain: Unitary system: sub-units subordinate -> central government can pass on orders; Federal system: state has powers of its own -> central government cannot order the state government

causeLinks.criterion: Contrasts the two systems: in a unitary system the central government can pass on orders to the provinces, while in a federal system it cannot order the state government.

concepts.label: Key Features of Federalism
concepts.cardText: In a federation there are two or more levels of government. They govern the same citizens, but each has its own jurisdiction in legislation, taxation and administration, specified in the constitution. Fundamental provisions cannot be changed by one level alone. Courts act as an umpire, sources of revenue are specified to ensure financial autonomy, and the system has dual objectives: unity and accommodating regional diversity.
concepts.hint: Think about levels, jurisdiction, the constitution, changes, courts, money and objectives.
concepts.probe: What are the key features of federalism?
concepts.causeChain: Jurisdiction guaranteed by the constitution + no unilateral changes + courts as umpire + financial autonomy -> each level's power is secure -> safeguard unity while accommodating regional diversity

causeLinks.criterion: Connects the constitutional guarantees of each level's power to the dual objectives of safeguarding unity and accommodating regional diversity.

keyPoints.text: There are two or more levels (or tiers) of government. Different tiers of government govern the same citizens, but each tier has its own jurisdiction in specific matters of legislation, taxation and administration.

concepts.label: Routes of Federalism: Coming Together vs Holding Together
concepts.cardText: Federations are formed in two ways. In 'coming together' federations, independent States come together on their own and pool sovereignty to increase their security; the States usually have equal power (USA, Switzerland, Australia). In 'holding together' federations, a large country divides its power between the constituent States and the national government; the central government tends to be more powerful (India, Spain, Belgium).
concepts.hint: Did independent States join together, or did one large country divide its power?
concepts.probe: Compare 'coming together' and 'holding together' federations. How does the balance of power differ?
concepts.causeChain: Independent States pool sovereignty to increase security -> coming together -> States usually have equal power; Large country divides its power -> holding together -> central government tends to be more powerful

causeLinks.criterion: Connects independent States coming together on their own to the States usually having equal power in such federations.
Connects a large country dividing its own power to the central government tending to be more powerful in such federations.

keyPoints.text: The first route involves independent States coming together on their own to form a bigger unit, so that by pooling sovereignty and retaining identity they can increase their security. This type of 'coming together' federations include the USA, Switzerland and Australia.

checks.criterion: States that in 'coming together' federations independent States come together on their own and pool sovereignty to form a bigger unit.

keyPoints.text: In this first category of federations, all the constituent States usually have equal power and are strong vis-à-vis the federal government.

checks.criterion: Mentions that in coming together federations the constituent States usually have equal power and are strong.
Gives an example of a coming together federation: USA, Switzerland or Australia.

keyPoints.text: The second route is where a large country decides to divide its power between the constituent States and the national government. India, Spain and Belgium are examples of this kind of 'holding together' federations.

requiredEvidence: large country decides to divide its power

checks.criterion: States that in 'holding together' federations a large country decides to divide its power between the constituent States and the national government.

topics.title: What makes India a federal country?

concepts.label: Union of States and Three-Fold Distribution
concepts.cardText: The Constitution declared India a Union of States based on the principles of federalism. It provided a three-fold distribution of legislative powers. The Union List has subjects of national importance (defence, foreign affairs, banking) that need a uniform policy. The State List has subjects of State and local importance (police, trade, agriculture). The Concurrent List has subjects of common interest (education, forest, marriage); if laws conflict, Union law prevails. The Union also legislates on 'residuary' subjects such as computer software.
concepts.hint: Think about the three lists, and what happens if the Centre and a State make conflicting laws on a shared subject.
concepts.probe: How does the Indian Constitution distribute legislative powers between the Union and State governments?
concepts.causeChain: Subjects need a uniform policy throughout the country -> Union List; subjects of State and local importance -> State List; subjects of common interest -> Concurrent List -> if laws conflict -> Union law prevails

causeLinks.criterion: Explains that the Union Government alone makes laws on Union List subjects because a uniform policy is needed on these matters throughout the country.

keyPoints.text: The Constitution declared India as a Union of States. Although it did not use the word federation, the Indian Union is based on the principles of federalism.

checks.criterion: States that the Constitution declared India a Union of States based on the principles of federalism.

keyPoints.text: The Constitution clearly provided a three-fold distribution of legislative powers. Union List includes subjects of national importance such as defence of the country, foreign affairs, banking, communications and currency. They are included in this list because we need a uniform policy on these matters throughout the country. The Union Government alone can make laws relating to these subjects.

checks.criterion: Mentions the State List (such as police or agriculture) and that only State Governments can make laws on it.

keyPoints.text: Concurrent List includes subjects of common interest to both the Union Government as well as the State Governments, such as education, forest, trade unions, marriage, adoption and succession. Both can make laws on these subjects. If their laws conflict with each other, the law made by the Union Government will prevail.
keyPoints.followUp: What is the Concurrent List, and what happens if laws made on it conflict?

checks.criterion: Mentions the Concurrent List (such as education or forest) on which both the Union and State governments can make laws.
States that if Union and State laws on a Concurrent subject conflict, the Union law prevails.

concepts.label: Amendment, Judiciary and Taxation
concepts.cardText: The Constitution originally provided for a two-tier system; a third tier was added later in the form of Panchayats and Municipalities. Parliament cannot change the power-sharing arrangement on its own: a change needs a two-thirds majority in both Houses, then ratification by the legislatures of at least half of the States. The High Courts and the Supreme Court decide disputes about the division of powers, and both the Union and State governments can raise resources by levying taxes.
concepts.hint: What has to happen before the power-sharing arrangement can be changed? Who settles disputes?
concepts.probe: How does the Constitution make it hard to change the federal power-sharing arrangement?
concepts.causeChain: Power sharing is basic to the Constitution -> Parliament cannot change it on its own -> change needs two-thirds of both Houses and ratification by half the States -> arrangement stays secure

causeLinks.criterion: Explains that Parliament cannot change the arrangement on its own because the change also needs ratification by the States.

keyPoints.text: The Constitution originally provided for a two-tier system of government, the Union Government and the State governments. Later, a third tier of federalism was added in the form of Panchayats and Municipalities.

concepts.label: Special Status and Union Territories
concepts.cardText: All States in the Indian Union do not have identical powers. Assam, Nagaland, Arunachal Pradesh and Mizoram enjoy special powers under Article 371 due to their peculiar social and historical circumstances, especially to protect land rights of indigenous peoples, their culture and preferential employment in government service. Areas too small to become a State that could not be merged with existing States, like Chandigarh, Lakshadweep and Delhi, are Union Territories; the Central Government has special powers in running them.

causeLinks.criterion: Connects the special status of some States under Article 371 to its purpose: protecting land rights of indigenous peoples, their culture or preferential employment.
Connects these areas being too small to become a State to the Central Government having special powers in running them.

Indians who are not permanent residents of these States cannot buy land or house there.

concepts.label: Linguistic States
concepts.cardText: The creation of linguistic States was the first and a major test for democratic politics in India. Boundaries of several old States were changed so that people who spoke the same language lived in the same State. Some States were created on the basis of culture, ethnicity or geography (Nagaland, Uttarakhand, Jharkhand). Some national leaders feared this would lead to the disintegration of the country, but it has actually made the country more united and made administration easier.

concepts.label: Language Policy
concepts.cardText: The Constitution did not give the status of national language to any one language. Hindi was identified as the official language, but it is the mother tongue of only about 40 per cent of Indians, so there are safeguards: 21 other Scheduled Languages, and States have their own official languages. English was to stop being used officially in 1965; non-Hindi speaking States demanded it continue, and in Tamil Nadu the movement took a violent form. The Centre agreed to continue English along with Hindi. This flexibility helped India avoid Sri Lanka's situation.

concepts.label: Centre-State Relations and Coalition Governments
concepts.cardText: For a long time the same party ruled at the Centre and in most States, and the Central Government would often misuse the Constitution to dismiss State governments controlled by rival parties. After 1990, regional parties rose in many States. With no single party getting a clear majority in the Lok Sabha, national parties had to form alliances with regional parties, leading to an era of coalition governments. This led to a new culture of power sharing and respect for the autonomy of State Governments, supported by a major Supreme Court judgement.

concepts.label: Decentralisation and the 1992 Amendment
concepts.cardText: When power is taken away from Central and State governments and given to local government, it is called decentralisation. Many problems are best settled at the local level: people know local problems and have better ideas on where to spend money. People can also participate directly in decision making, which builds a habit of democratic participation. Local government realises the principle of local self-government. Before 1992, local bodies were under the direct control of State governments, without regular elections or resources of their own. The 1992 amendment made elections regular, reserved seats (one-third for women), created State Election Commissions and required States to share some powers and revenue.

concepts.label: Panchayati Raj and Urban Local Bodies
concepts.cardText: Rural local government is known as Panchayati Raj. Each village, or group of villages, has a gram panchayat: ward members (panch) and a president (sarpanch), directly elected by the adult population. It works under the supervision of the gram sabha, made up of all the voters in the village. A few gram panchayats form a panchayat samiti (block or mandal), whose members are elected by all the panchayat members in that area. All the panchayat samitis in a district form the zilla parishad. Towns have municipalities and big cities have municipal corporations, controlled by elected bodies and headed by the chairperson or mayor.

concepts.probe: Describe the structure of Panchayati Raj, from the village to the district.

keyPoints.text: Rural local government is popularly known by the name Panchayati Raj. Each village, or a group of villages in some States, has a gram panchayat. This is a council consisting of several ward members, often called panch, and a president or sarpanch. They are directly elected by all the adult population living in that ward or village. It is the decision-making body for the entire village.

keyPoints.text: The panchayat works under the overall supervision of the gram sabha. All the voters in the village are its members. It has to meet at least twice or thrice in a year to approve the annual budget of the gram panchayat and to review the performance of the gram panchayat.

checks.criterion: Explains that the gram sabha is made up of all the voters in the village and supervises the gram panchayat (approving its budget and reviewing its performance).

checks.criterion: Mentions that a few gram panchayats are grouped together to form a panchayat samiti (block or mandal).

keyPoints.text: All the panchayat samitis or mandals in a district together constitute the zilla (district) parishad. Most members of the zilla parishad are elected. Members of the Lok Sabha and MLAs of that district and some other officials of other district level bodies are also its members. Zilla parishad chairperson is the political head of the zilla parishad.

checks.criterion: Mentions that all the panchayat samitis in a district together constitute the zilla parishad.

keyPoints.text: Local government bodies exist for urban areas as well. Municipalities are set up in towns. Big cities are constituted into municipal corporations. Both municipalities and municipal corporations are controlled by elected bodies consisting of people's representatives. Municipal chairperson is the political head of the municipality. In a municipal corporation such an officer is called the mayor.

concepts.label: Local Government: Achievements and Shortcomings
concepts.cardText: The new system of local government is the largest experiment in democracy conducted anywhere in the world, with about 36 lakh elected representatives. Constitutional status has helped deepen democracy and increased women's representation and voice. But gram sabhas are not held regularly, and most State governments have not transferred significant powers or adequate resources to local governments. We are still a long way from realising the ideal of self-government.
